name: PAPAGENO (PArallel PArser GENeratOr)
baseline: GNU Bison + GNU Flex (sequential LALR(1) parser/lexer)
workload: Lexing+AST-construction of real-world JSON files (2.7KiB-75MiB: AdBlocker config, Gospel of John, Italian food-consumption stats, Google Books n-gram stats, UK CKAN index) and Lua files (7KiB-35MiB, from the Grim Fandango remaster codebase), on a 16-core x86_64 Opteron server and a 4x Cortex-A15/4x Cortex-A7 ARM board.
claimed_speedup: Text says parallel PAPAGENO-generated lexer+parser gets 'a significant speedup with respect to the state-of-the-art tool generated parsers [Flex+Bison], for all but the smallest test-bench files', and on the ARM (RISC) platform 'a speedup of up to 5.5x ... combination of the parallel processing technique on multiple cores and the lesser computational requirements with respect to a classic LALR(1) parser.' Figure 13b (JSON, x86 server) shows peak speedup vs Flex-Bison reaching roughly 7x at high worker counts (derived from page data, chart axis).
hardware: Server: quad-Opteron 8378 (16 physical cores, 4 sockets), Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64. Mobile: Odroid-XU Lite, Exynos 5 Octa (4x Cortex-A15 @1.4GHz + 4x Cortex-A7, big.LITTLE, using only the 4 A15 cores), Debian 7.6 armv7l.
tradeoffs: Requires the grammar to be restructured as an Operator Precedence Grammar (a strict subset of LALR(1)); converting a real LALR(1) Lua grammar to OPG+Fischer-normal-form blew productions up from 144 to 8547; Lua required manual token-disambiguation and semicolon-insertion transforms in the lexer; parser is generated as C source using POSIX threads, so parallelism only pays off once input is large enough (small files show little or negative speedup from thread migration/NUMA overhead).
caveats: Benchmark authored by the tool's own developers, comparing against a Flex+Bison reference parser they built themselves (not the JSON/Lua ecosystem's own production parsers); smallest test files show negligible or no speedup; only Operator-Precedence-compatible grammars are supported, not general context-free/ambiguous grammars that Bison's GLR mode or ANTLR can handle; project has had no commits since 2015.
found_via: WebSearch: 'parallel LR parsing multicore faster than bison paper' -> Barenghi, Crespi Reghizzi, Mandrioli, Panella, Pradella, 'Parallel Parsing Made Practical', Science of Computer Programming 2016 (open-access PDF via Politecnico di Milano repository); repo confirmed via its README matching the paper's authors and toolchain description.

name: flap (fused lexing and parsing)
baseline: ocamlyacc (also benchmarked against Menhir's table- and code-generation backends)
workload: Six real grammars benchmarked with Core_bench: Portable Game Notation (pgn), Netpbm PPM images (ppm), S-expressions (sexp), CSV (csv, Shafranovich RFC), JSON (json), and a small arithmetic/binding language (arith); linear-time parsing confirmed across input sizes from ~0.1MB to tens of MB.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: flap 'generates specialized token-free code that runs two to six times faster than ocamlyacc on a range of benchmarks.' Figure 11 throughput numbers (MB/s) on the page: json flap=1359 vs ocamlyacc=236 (~5.8x, derived from page data) and vs menhir+code=326 (~4.2x, derived); csv flap=323 vs ocamlyacc=76 (~4.25x, derived); pgn flap=286 vs ocamlyacc=67 (~4.3x, derived); sexp flap=213 vs ocamlyacc=76 (~2.8x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: BER MetaOCaml N111 with flambda optimizations enabled
hardware: Single core of an Intel i9-12900K, 1GB memory, Debian Linux.
tradeoffs: OCaml-only (uses MetaOCaml staging), not usable from C/C++; grammars are limited to deterministic context-free expressions with a single token of lookahead (DGNF), so fully ambiguous/GLR-style grammars are out of scope; Greibach Normal Form conversion plus lexer/parser fusion can duplicate grammar productions, increasing generated code size.
caveats: Baseline is ocamlyacc/menhir (OCaml-ecosystem yacc-family tools), not Bison/ANTLR/Boost.Spirit/nom directly, though ocamlyacc is architecturally the same class of tool as Bison; single-core, single-CPU-model microbenchmark; peer-reviewed at PLDI 2023 with a public Zenodo artifact (10.5281/zenodo.7824835), so results are independently reproducible; project repo has had no commits since shortly after the PLDI 2023 camera-ready.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Menhir OCaml parser generator faster than yacc bison benchmark' -> Yallop, Xie, Krishnaswami, 'flap: A Deterministic Parser with Fused Lexing', PLDI 2023 / arXiv:2304.05276.

name: Pika Parser (reference implementation)
workload: (1) 2,500 random arithmetic expressions (integers, binary ops, unary negation, parens), input lengths 5 chars to 4.8MB; (2) 5,372 real Java 6 source files from the Spring framework (avg 3.8KiB, max 76KiB, comments stripped).
claimed_speedup: For the arithmetic-expression grammar, the paper states pika parsing was 'roughly the same speed' as ANTLR4/Parboiled2 for small inputs but became '10 times faster than ANTLR4' and '1000 times faster than Parboiled2' for large expressions (ANTLR4 scaled as ~n^1.21, Parboiled2 as ~n^1.9, pika as linear). For the Java grammar, the relationship reverses: the paper states pika parsing was 'up to 1000, 100 or 10 times slower' than ANTLR4 depending on input length, and about 100x slower than Parboiled2, because of a large per-character constant-factor overhead on complex grammars.
tradeoffs: Result is strongly grammar-dependent: faster than ANTLR4/Parboiled2 only for simple/shallow grammars (expression grammar) and markedly slower for large, deeply-nested grammars like Java's; pika parsing's benefit is mainly linear-time guarantee plus built-in left-recursion support and syntax-error recovery, not raw speed on complex languages; memoizes every rule at every position, which costs memory.
caveats: Not a universal speed win -- the same paper shows it is slower than both baselines on the Java grammar; the repository's public test suite (src/test/java/pikaparser/Benchmark.java) reproduces the Parboiled2 comparison, but no ANTLR4 comparison harness was found in the same repo, so the ANTLR4 numbers are not independently re-runnable from this exact codebase; published at SLE 2020 (peer-reviewed workshop), keeping it at tier B rather than A.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Pika parsing faster than packrat ANTLR arxiv' -> Hutchison, 'Pika parsing: reformulating packrat parsing as a dynamic programming algorithm solves the left recursion and error recovery problems', arXiv:2005.06444 / SLE 2020.

name: MPL / FastParse (kurotakazuki/mpl)
baseline: nom (also benchmarked against pest, peg, winnow, chumsky, serde_json)
workload: Recognition-only (bool match, no AST construction) micro-benchmarks: nested-parenthesis matching at depth 1024/4096 with no backtracking; JSON/canada/citm recognition corpora; and left-recursive-sum ('lsum') grammars at sizes 64/256/1024.
claimed_speedup: README claims MPL's static-codegen backend 'beats pest, peg, nom, winnow, and chumsky on equal-work benchmarks, and even beats serde_json on equal-work recognition benchmarks.' Reported Criterion numbers: nested-parens depth 1024, MPL 2.26us vs nom 7.50us (~3.3x, derived from page data); depth 4096, MPL 9.23us vs nom 20.8us (~2.25x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo/rustc with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"; criterion 0.8.2, sample size 100; dependency versions pinned (pest 2.8.6, peg 0.8.6, winnow 1.0.3, nom 8.0.0, chumsky 0.13.0), re-run 2026-05-30.
tradeoffs: Very new, minimally-adopted grammar formalism (single-rule TDPL/GTDPL, `.mplg` DSL + macro), far less battle-tested than nom; benchmarks are recognition-only (returns bool), so they do not measure the cost of building an actual parse tree/AST, which is what most real nom users need; single maintainer.
caveats: First-party benchmark written and run by the sole maintainer, not independently reproduced; no CPU model is stated (only compiler flags and library versions), so this falls short of tier A/B by this run's rules; adoption is minimal (6 GitHub stars) despite the strong claims, so treat as a lead to verify rather than an established result.
found_via: WebSearch: 'FastParse Rust TDPL PEG static-codegen faster than nom pest winnow benchmark github' -> kurotakazuki/mpl README benchmark table.
